title: What squatter cities can teach us
speaker: Stewart Brand

keyTerms.definition: about the population: how many people, and where they live
an area where people build homes on land they don't own, often without official planning
the moment when a small change causes a big change
basic systems such as roads, water pipes and power
the total value of everything a country or region produces

predictionQuestion: Millions of people move from villages to informal city areas. Do you think this is good or bad? What might the speaker argue?

keyIdeas.text: A major population change is happening: the world is passing 50% urban. This may be an economic tipping point.
The biggest cities used to be Western cities like Paris, London and New York. That has changed.
Villages around the world are emptying out as people move to cities.
Most people go to squatter cities, not to big modern centres.
People in squatter cities are not trapped by poverty. They are getting out of poverty as fast as they can.
The residents build and design these places themselves, with home-made infrastructure and lively street life.
Example: Mumbai produces about one-sixth of India's GDP.
In squatter cities everyone works, and education is a key benefit of city life.
His first punch line: cities have defused the population bomb.
Final image: stars have shone on Earth for billions of years; now city lights shine back up.

modelNotes: - old biggest cities = West (Paris, London, NY) → no longer
- ppl getting OUT of poverty fast (not trapped)
- residents build + design; home-made infrastructure; lively street life
- 2. city lights 'shine back up' at the stars

Cities around the world are getting smaller

questions.stem: According to the talk, where do most people leaving villages go?
options: To big modern cities like Shanghai
questions.explanation: He says some go to places like Shanghai, but most go to squatter cities.

options: They are getting out of poverty quickly
